title: tensorrt-triton-custom-kernel-integration-experiments-notes
content:
Status: draft
Authors: Lina Chen (owner) + Ravi Kumar, Elena Garcia, Tom Anders
Context: ongoing evaluation of options to integrate TensorRT-optimized kernels and Triton-based serving with our custom kernel paths. Goal is to find a pragmatic integration strategy that yields low P50/P95 token latency, high GPU utilization, and manageable engineering/ops complexity for Redwood Dedicated and Private deployments.

Summary and goals:
- Problem: model variants and quantized artifacts perform best with custom kernels (optimized GEMM, fused attention) in TensorRT, but our runtime needs: scheduling, dynamic batching, KV cache sharing, and transparent fallback to non-TensorRT paths (e.g., CPU or alternative kernels).
- Goals:
  - Get stable end-to-end inference with TensorRT kernels behind Triton and our runtime abstraction.
  - Keep latency SLOs (P50 < 20ms token for short seqs on A10x) and P95 within 2x P50 for most workloads.
  - Maintain KV cache correctness and fast context-switch for multi-tenant workloads.
  - Keep engineering complexity reasonable (avoid large forked codepaths).

High-level approaches we experimented with:
1) Triton as the primary serving surface + TensorRT backends (recommended path)
   - Triton does model loading, lifecycle, and exposes gRPC/HTTP. Use TensorRT backend for optimized engines.
   - Pros: mature lifecycle, auto-reload, GPU memory management, concurrent instance model (CIM) controls. Leverages Triton batching primitives.
   - Cons: Triton batching semantics differ from our continuous-batching runtime. Integrating KV cache (sequence generation with incremental decoding) required a custom control protocol.

2) Direct TensorRT integration inside our runtime (custom kernel path)
   - Our runtime directly loads TensorRT engines and manages inference calls, batching, and pipeline.
   - Pros: tight control over batching, easier to integrate our KV cache and continuous-decoding flow, minimal RPC overhead.
   - Cons: reimplement lifecycle (engine reloads), driver edge cases, more ops surface to support in Dedicated/Private. More maintenance burden for engine building and plugin compatibility.

3) Hybrid: Triton for model lifecycle + our router for per-token scheduling, with custom per-request transport to TensorRT engines (bypass Triton inference path)
   - Triton maintains model files and builds TensorRT engines. Our runtime calls into the same TensorRT engine via shared GPU memory or IPC.
   - Pros: separation of concerns; less duplication.
   - Cons: complex IPC, synchronization for engine access, pointer stability across Triton reboots.

Experiments we ran (short notes):
- Baselines: FP16 vs INT8 engines, with and without fused attention kernel, on A10/A100. Generated engines with TensorRT 8.5 and 9.0 nightlies.
- Throughput/latency microbenchmarks: 8 batch sizes (1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128) with seq lengths {8,64,512}. Measured token latency (cold vs warm), end-to-end call latency (runtime + kernel), and KV cache lookup overhead.
- Mixed workload: concurrent small chat requests (many short sequences) + occasional long context eval (512) to stress scheduling.
- Failure modes: Triton model-reload while engine-in-use, plugin-incompatibility after driver update, CUDA OOM patterns when many model variants loaded.

Selected results (representative):
- FP16 fused kernels (TensorRT) on A100:
  - Batch=1, seq=8: kernel-only P50=3.1ms, end-to-end P50=9.2ms (our runtime overhead ~6ms for KV + token handling).
  - Batch=8, seq=64: throughput up to 280 tokens/s per GPU with ~14ms kernel P50.
- INT8 aggressive quant on A10 (calibrated):
  - Batch=1, seq=8: kernel-only P50=2.6ms, but occasional quality drop on rare tokens; end-to-end P95 spikes observed due to re-calibration/fallback paths.
- Triton path vs direct integration:
  - Triton adds ~1.5-3ms RPC/transport overhead for small batch sizes; overhead amortized on larger batches.
  - Continuous-batching mismatch: Triton’s batch-collect (requests -> batch) timing caused slight extra jitter for P95 in high QPS short-request workloads. Direct integration reduced jitter but increased operational risk.

KV cache integration notes:
- Challenge: TensorRT engines operate on a fixed compute model (single-call inputs -> outputs). For autoregressive decoding, we need to feed past KV states and get new KV outputs. Options:
  1) Expose KV tensors as inputs/outputs at engine boundary (preferred): design engine input schema: {input_ids, past_key_value_buffers, attention_mask} -> outputs include logits and new KV slices. Requires careful memory layout and plugin support for dynamic sizes.
  2) Host-side KV stitching: run attention kernel for current token; maintain KV on host, use repeat/unroll. Simpler but incurs H2D/D2H overhead and kernel inefficiency.
  3) Shared GPU memory KV store: runtime and engine share CUDA-allocated buffers (CUDA IPC or unified memory) and engine reads/writes in-place. Fastest in theory but brittle across process boundaries and Triton-managed lifecycles.
- From experiments: (1) is best for single-process direct TensorRT integration; (3) works only after substantial engine lifecycle/ops work and only in dedicated deployments. (2) is simplest fallback for Private deployments where Triton is used as a strict boundary.

Scheduling and batching consequences:
- Continuous batching (our current runtime) expects to append tokens incrementally and drive kernel calls frequently. TensorRT prefers collecting bigger micro-batches to amortize kernel launch. Tradeoff: latency vs throughput.
- We prototyped a hybrid scheduler that: tries to honor P50 latency by micro-batching small windows for short requests (timeout < 5ms) and aggregates longer windows for background workloads. This reduces P95 jitter while preserving throughput.
- For Triton: rely on Triton batching but add a thin pre-aggregator that coalesces our micro-batches into Triton request batches. This worked but required careful timeout tuning.

Operational & engineering tradeoffs:
- Complexity: Direct TensorRT gives best perf for tight latency targets but requires us to take on engine building/compatibility matrix and release coordination (TensorRT versions, CUDA versions).
- Triton reduces ops burden (model reloading, multi-instance), more robust for multi-tenant Dedicated environments. But it can introduce jitter and makes KV sharing harder if Triton is used as strict RPC boundary.
- Hybrid/shared-engine approach solves some ops duplication but increases coupling between Triton and our runtime—hard to validate across upgrades.
- Fallback story: must implement automatic fallback to non-TensorRT engines on engine load failures, and metricized quality checks for INT8 models.

Open questions and TODOs:
- Plugin strategy: build a stable fused-attention TRT plugin that accepts variable KV shapes (action: Ravi to prototype plugin ABI by 2025-10-24).
- Engine lifecycle: how to safely invalidate/replace engines without impacting in-flight requests? Policy options: reference-counted engines, drain semantics in Triton, or short-circuit reroute to CPU path.
- KV memory ownership model: choose between in-engine KV (safer perf) vs shared GPU KV buffers (better multi-process support). Need SRE input for memory accounting (Elena follow-up).
- Quantization QA: build automatic eval harness for output deltas at token-level; tie to rollouts (Tom to add gating in rollout system).

Recommended near-term path (pragmatic):
1) For Hosted API and Dedicated we default to Triton + TensorRT backend for model lifecycle, with a lightweight pre-aggregator in the runtime that coalesces short micro-batches into Triton batches (reduce jitter).
2) For Dedicated high-performance SKUs and Private on-prem customers who opt-in, provide a direct-TensorRT runtime binary option (feature flag) that uses in-engine KV tensors for max perf. Document compatibility and support boundary.
3) Implement engine-fallbacks and a quantization QA gate before auto-rollout of INT8 engines.

Short-term milestones (next 6 weeks):
- Prototype fused-attention TRT plugin with KV_in/KV_out ABI (Ravi, 2w).
- Implement pre-aggregator for Triton path and measure P50/P95 across workloads (Lina + Tom, 3w).
- Add engine-fallback plumbing and rollout gating for INT8 (Tom, 4w).
- Ops doc for engine lifecycle and memory accounting (Elena, 6w).

Unresolved notes / rough ideas:
- Could we use a lightweight in-process Triton embed (libtriton) to get model lifecycle with lower RPC overhead? Investigate.
- Consider a small persistent KV service per-GPU that kernels can read/write; might help multi-process isolation.

Appendix: quick links
- PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/412 (triton pre-aggregator prototype), https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/418 (trt fused-kernel experiments)
- Bench harness: internal/bench/tensorrt-kernel-suite (see Confluence link)
